17. Mr ASM Abdul Mubin the learned Assistant Attorney-General at the out set submits that in the instant case the place of occurrence and time of occurrence has not been challenged by the defence. With reference to the first information report, he has pointed out that Exhibit 1 and 3 are the first information report in this case although the original first information report has unfortunately been lost in the case. Referring to the defects as noted in respect of first information report Mr Mobin placed reliance in the case of Somappa vs State of Mysore reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 1831 (1836 para 12) wherefrom he submits that even rejection of the first information report would not detract the testimonies of the eye-witnesses which can be assessed independently. Mr Mobin submits further that the first information report has got a presumption about the correctness in its favour under section 114( e) of the Evidence Act, therefore whatever defect as pointed out over the same it is incumbent upon the defence to rebut the presumption as contemplated under section 114( e) of the Evidence At. In support of his contention he then placed reliance in the case of Sonilal vs State of Uttar Prodesh reported in AIR 1978 (SC) 1142 (1143 para 11). 

 22. Mr Md Hannan, the learned Advocate appearing as State Defence Lawyer on behalf of the absconding condemned prisoners, submits that the complicity of 2 out of 3 condemned prisoners i.e. Dafader Marfat Ali Shah, Ld (Dafader Abul Hashem Mridha could not be proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt, in that PW 1 Kazi Abdul Awal deposed to the effect that all the 5 army personnel put their signatures in the register at the Jail Gate before they had entered inside the Jail. Despite specific suggestion put to this witness (PW1) in this regard the prosecution did not produce the said register before the Court to prove the complicity of these .two convicts rather the said register has been deliberately withheld by the prosecution warranting adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act against the prosecution case. Mr Hannan submits further that the so-called first information report was registered 36 hours after the occurrence yet the same contains only one name i.e Moslemuddin but the other two were not even named in the said first information report It is also submitted by Mr Hannan that Exhibit 2 is said to be a detailed report submitted by PW I DIG (Prisons) addressing the Inspector General of Prisons on 5-11-1975 but the said detailed report too, does not disclose the name of the said two condemned prisoners. It is also submitted by him that PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 21 do not disclose the complicity of Dafader Marfat Ali Shah, Ld. (Dafader) Abul Hashem Mridha. 

 46. Pointing out the cross-examination portion of the witnesses Mr Syed Mizanur Rahman submits that the duty register of Bangabhaban in respect of PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 showing them as employees of Bangabhaban at the relevant time was deliberately withheld by the prosecution warranting adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. 

 269. Under the given circumstances, the telephonic conversations from Bangabhaban to Central Jail as disclosed by the witnesses is very much difficult to be believed. Moreover, we find no reason to dis-agree with the learned Sessions Judge who after thorough analysis of their depositions found the testimonies of PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 as unworthy of credence in the first part of his impugned judgment although he has contradicted his own findings at the later part of the same judgment. It is also evident from the deposition of PW 17 that the President could himself call anyone from his personal phone and that the President had his Military Secretary who used to remain at the disposal of the President round the clock and PW 17 and others had no authority to move a step without the permission from the Military Secretary and the ADC of the President. This witness appears to have disclosed the name of the Military Secretary wrongly. This also indicates that had he been in any service at Bangabhaban at the relevant time there was no reason why he should not know the name of the Military Secretary to the President, moreover these witnesses i.e PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 were specifically suggested that they were not in service of Bangabhaban at the relevant time, though the suggestions were denied by this witnesses. Admitting to the effect that they had put their signatures in the duty register maintained at Bangabhaban, it was also suggested from the side of the defence that the duty register does not bear their signatures evidencing that they were on duty at the relevant time yet the duty register was not produced before the Court despite specific suggestion made to the witnesses in this regard. Non production of the duty register of Bangabhaban showing the signatures of this witnesses namely, PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 warrants an adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. These circumstances coupled with the deposition of the witnesses as referred to above lead us to believe that the testimonies of those witnesses namely, PWs 11, 13, 16, 17, 18 and 34 are not trustworthy. We do not, in this regard find any reason to discard the finding of the trial Court in respect of the testimonies of those witnesses as available in the 1st part of his impugned judgment. 

 This piece of evidence lends support to the defence version of the case and in a position like this the case of Muslimuddin vs State reported in 38 DLR (AD) 311 may be referred to wherefrom we find that the principle laid down in that case is that the fundamental principle of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduce evidence to prove his innocence, but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence continues, whether the case is before the trial Court or at higher forums..........................................................................................In a criminal case it is the duty of the Court to review the entire evidence that has been produced by the prosecution and the defence, if after an examination of the whole evidence, the Court is of opinion that there is reasonable possibility that the defence put forward by the accused might be true, it is clear that such a view reacts on the whole prosecution case. In these circumstances the accused is entitled to benefit of doubt, not as a matter of grace but as of right, because the prosecution has not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. 

 303. Turning to the case of 3 condemned prisoners, we find that they are (1) Resalder Moslemuddin alias Muslemuddin (Retd) alias Hiron Khan alias Muslemuddin (absconding) (2) Dafader Marfat Ali Shah (absconding) and (3) LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha (absconding). From the prosecution witnesses cited from the Central Jail, Dhaka none of them mentioned their names i.e the aforesaid two persons. In Exhibit 1 which was said to be the first information report. lodged first in point of time on 4-11-1975 that information does not contain names of two condemned prisoners i.e Dafader Marfat Ali Saha and LD (Dafader) Md Abul Hashem Mridha. Moreover PW 1 the informant has asserted in his deposition to the effect that all the 5 assailants who had gone to the Jail Gate and subsequently committed murder of the 4 leaders put their signatures in the gate register before their entrance inside the Jail and this PW 1 himself in his deposition in chief disclosed that it was at his asking all the 5 assailants put their signatures in the gate register, if. that be so in that case the gate register could have been the most vital document to connect all 5 assailants in this case but unfortunately, for the prosecution that gate register was not produced before the Court, therefore, it is rightly submitted by Mr Hannan that it warrants an adverse presumption in the prosecution case under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act.
